name: Battle of Poitiers (1356)

phases.title: The two armies take their ground
phases.text: The Anglo-Gascons held a wooded hill, the Prince's division behind the other two as a reserve. The French drew up in four divisions, the first about 500 yards from the English.

phases.title: The French cavalry charge the two wings
phases.text: Audrehem's horsemen rode at Warwick's division and Clermont's at Salisbury's. On the left the marsh kept them from the archers. On the right they reached the gap in the hedge and a fierce melee began.

phases.title: The first division is beaten and the second attacks
phases.text: The cavalry were driven back with heavy losses and the first division was forced to withdraw under the English archers' fire. The second division, 4,000 strong, then attacked at the hedge, and the Prince committed his reserve.

phases.title: The Dauphin's division withdraws, and Orléans leaves
phases.text: After two hours the Dauphin's division withdrew in order. Orléans marched away with half of the third division. The rest made a feeble attack that was easily repelled, and some of Warwick's men left their line in pursuit.

phases.title: The King's division advances; the Captal rides round
phases.text: The King's division, swelled by survivors of the earlier attacks, marched across the gap with the Oriflamme unfurled. The Anglo-Gascons sent a small mounted force under the Captal de Buch round the French flank.

phases.title: The Prince orders a general advance
phases.text: The Black Prince ordered a general advance and the Anglo-Gascons moved out of their position. Warwick's men returning from the pursuit reinforced the line as the Captal's force worked round to the French rear.

phases.title: The French are attacked from behind and break
phases.text: The Captal's 160 men struck the French rear. The division fell apart, and those still fighting around the King were forced into a loop of the River Miosson. They were surrounded, and John and his youngest son surrendered.

note: The accounts do not give compass directions, so the plan has the French at the top and the English at the bottom. The hedge, the marsh and the River Miosson are placed by judgement: the accounts say the marsh lay by Warwick's archers on the English left and the hedge before Salisbury's men on the right, but not exactly where. The French rear divisions stood behind the leading one; their sideways positions are not given. The Captal de Buch's route round the flank, and the side it took, are not given either. Warwick's and Salisbury's divisions are each drawn as one block with their archers.
